name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH06_MATCH_LIST_Q01 - Moments of inertia of symmetrical bodies

questiontext.text:
Match the physical body and axis of rotation in List-I with its corresponding moment of inertia in List-II (where \(M\) is mass, \(R\) is radius, and \(L\) is length):

List-I (Body and Axis) List-II (Moment of Inertia)
(A) Thin circular ring of radius \(R\) about central perpendicular axis (I) \(\frac{1}{12}ML^2\)
(B) Circular disc of radius \(R\) about its diameter (II) \(MR^2\)
(C) Thin uniform rod of length \(L\) about perpendicular axis through midpoint (III) \(\frac{2}{5}MR^2\)
(D) Uniform solid sphere of radius \(R\) about its diameter (IV) \(\frac{1}{4}MR^2\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of thin circular ring about central perpendicular axis
For a thin circular ring of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\), all mass elements are situated at a constant perpendicular distance \(R\) from the axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to the ring plane. Integrating over all mass elements gives \(I = \sum m_i r_i^2 = MR^2\). This matches with Roman numeral II.

Step 2: Evaluation of circular disc about its diameter
For a uniform circular disc of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\), the moment of inertia about the central perpendicular axis is \(I_z = \frac{1}{2}MR^2\). By the perpendicular axes theorem for a planar laminar body, \(I_x + I_y = I_z\). Due to circular symmetry about any coplanar diameter, \(I_x = I_y = I_d\). Therefore, \(2I_d = \frac{1}{2}MR^2\), which yields \(I_d = \frac{1}{4}MR^2\). This matches with Roman numeral IV.

Step 3: Evaluation of thin uniform rod about perpendicular axis through midpoint
For a thin uniform rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\), taking the origin at the centre gives linear mass density \(\lambda = \frac{M}{L}\). Integrating \(\mathrm{d}I = x^2\,\mathrm{d}m = \lambda x^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) from \(x = -L/2\) to \(x = +L/2\) yields \(I = \frac{M}{L}\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-L/2}^{L/2} = \frac{1}{12}ML^2\). This matches with Roman numeral I.

Step 4: Evaluation of uniform solid sphere about its diameter
For a uniform solid sphere of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\), integrating coaxial thin elemental discs along the diameter yields the standard moment of inertia \(I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2\). This matches with Roman numeral III.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Combining each matched pair consistently gives the overall matching: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH06_MATCH_LIST_Q02 - Translational and rotational kinematic dynamic analogues

questiontext.text:
Match each translational physical quantity in List-I with its corresponding rotational analogue in List-II:

List-I (Translational Quantity) List-II (Rotational Analogue)
(A) Linear momentum (\(\mathbf{p}\)) (I) Moment of inertia (\(I\))
(B) Force (\(\mathbf{F}\)) (II) Angular momentum (\(\mathbf{L}\))
(C) Linear mass (\(M\)) (III) Angular velocity (\(\boldsymbol{\omega}\))
(D) Linear velocity (\(\mathbf{v}\)) (IV) Torque (\(\boldsymbol{\tau}\))

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analogue of linear momentum
Linear momentum is defined as \(\mathbf{p} = M\mathbf{v}\) and represents the quantity of translational motion. Its rotational counterpart represents the moment of momentum about a reference point or axis, defined as angular momentum \(\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} = I\boldsymbol{\omega}\). This matches with Roman numeral II.

Step 2: Analogue of force
Force represents the rate of change of linear momentum in translational dynamics, \(\mathbf{F} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{p}}{\mathrm{d}t}\). The rotational analogue causing angular acceleration and governing the rate of change of angular momentum is torque, \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}}{\mathrm{d}t}\). This matches with Roman numeral IV.

Step 3: Analogue of mass
Mass \(M\) is the measure of inertia in translational motion, resisting changes in linear velocity. In rotational motion about a fixed axis, the measure of rotational inertia resisting changes in angular velocity is the moment of inertia \(I = \sum m_i r_i^2\). This matches with Roman numeral I.

Step 4: Analogue of linear velocity
Linear velocity is the time rate of change of linear displacement, \(\mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}{\mathrm{d}t}\). Its rotational counterpart, describing the time rate of angular displacement, is angular velocity \(\boldsymbol{\omega} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\mathrm{d}t}\). This matches with Roman numeral III.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Combining each matched pair consistently gives the overall matching: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH06_MATCH_LIST_Q03 - Dimensions of rotational physical quantities

questiontext.text:
Match the physical quantities related to rotational motion in List-I with their dimensional formulae in List-II:

List-I (Physical Quantity) List-II (Dimensional Formula)
(A) Angular momentum (I) \([\mathrm{M\,L^2}]\)
(B) Torque (II) \([\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]\)
(C) Moment of inertia (III) \([\mathrm{T^{-2}}]\)
(D) Angular acceleration (IV) \([\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-1}}]\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Dimensional formula of angular momentum
Angular momentum is defined as \(\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p}\). Dimensionally, \([L] = [\text{length}] \times [\text{momentum}] = [\mathrm{L}] \times [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-1}}] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-1}}]\). This matches with Roman numeral IV.

Step 2: Dimensional formula of torque
Torque is defined as \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\). Dimensionally, \([\tau] = [\text{length}] \times [\text{force}] = [\mathrm{L}] \times [\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}] = [\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-2}}]\). This matches with Roman numeral II.

Step 3: Dimensional formula of moment of inertia
Moment of inertia is defined as \(I = \sum m_i r_i^2\). Dimensionally, \([I] = [\text{mass}] \times [\text{length}]^2 = [\mathrm{M\,L^2}]\). This matches with Roman numeral I.

Step 4: Dimensional formula of angular acceleration
Angular acceleration is defined as \(\boldsymbol{\alpha} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\mathrm{d}t}\). Since angular displacement is dimensionless, angular velocity has dimensions \([\mathrm{T^{-1}}]\), and angular acceleration has dimensions \(\frac{[\mathrm{T^{-1}}]}{[\mathrm{T}]} = [\mathrm{T^{-2}}]\) (or \([\mathrm{M^0\,L^0\,T^{-2}}]\)). This matches with Roman numeral III.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Combining each matched pair consistently gives the overall matching: A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH06_MATCH_LIST_Q04 - Locations of centre of mass of bodies

questiontext.text:
Match the physical system described in List-I with the location of its centre of mass in List-II:

List-I (Physical System) List-II (Location of Centre of Mass)
(A) Three equal point masses placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side \(a\) (I) Distance \(\frac{L}{2}\) from either end
(B) Uniform thin rod of length \(L\) (II) At the centroid, at distance \(\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\) from each vertex
(C) Uniform circular ring of radius \(R\) (III) On the median, at distance \(\frac{h}{3}\) from the base
(D) Uniform triangular lamina of height \(h\) (IV) At the geometric centre, where no material is present

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of three equal point masses at vertices of equilateral triangle
Let the three identical masses \(m\) be placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side \(a\). By symmetry, the centre of mass lies at the centroid of the triangle. The distance from any vertex to the centroid along the median of length \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a\) is given by \(\frac{2}{3} \times \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a\right) = \frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\). This matches with Roman numeral II.

Step 2: Evaluation of uniform thin rod of length \(L\)
For a uniform thin straight rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\), linear mass density is constant. Integrating \(X_{\mathrm{cm}} = \frac{1}{M}\int_0^L x\,\lambda\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{L}\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^L = \frac{L}{2}\). Thus, the centre of mass lies at the geometric midpoint, at a distance \(\frac{L}{2}\) from either end. This matches with Roman numeral I.

Step 3: Evaluation of uniform circular ring of radius \(R\)
By circular symmetry about any diameter, the centre of mass of a uniform thin circular ring lies at its geometric centre. Because the ring consists of matter only along its circumference, the geometric centre lies in the empty space enclosed by the ring where no material is present. This matches with Roman numeral IV.

Step 4: Evaluation of uniform triangular lamina of height \(h\)
A uniform triangular lamina can be considered as a collection of thin strips parallel to its base. The centre of mass of each strip lies at its midpoint, so the centre of mass of the whole lamina lies along the median connecting the vertex to the base midpoint. Integrating strips along the altitude from the base gives the centroid at a vertical distance of \(\frac{h}{3}\) from the base. This matches with Roman numeral III.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Combining each matched pair consistently gives the overall matching: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.
